subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: China's former one-child policy is an example of:
questions.explain: The one-child policy aimed to reduce births, making it an anti-natalist population policy.

questions.q: The 'site' of a settlement refers to:
options: Its position relative to other places
The actual land on which it is built
questions.explain: Site describes the physical land a settlement is built on, while situation describes its position relative to surroundings.

questions.q: The function of a settlement describes:
options: The land it is built on
The main activity or purpose it serves
questions.explain: A settlement's function is its main purpose, such as a market town, port, industrial centre or tourist resort.

questions.q: Which is an example of a 'push' factor for migration?
options: Conflict or persecution in the home country
A safe and peaceful environment in the destination
questions.explain: Push factors drive people away from their home area; conflict and persecution are common push factors.

questions.q: Natural increase in a population occurs when:
options: Birth rate is higher than death rate
Death rate is higher than birth rate
questions.explain: Natural increase is when births exceed deaths, causing the population to grow before migration is considered.

questions.q: The 'situation' of a settlement refers to its:
options: Physical land it is built on
Position relative to surrounding features and other places
questions.explain: Situation describes where a settlement lies in relation to its surroundings, such as routes, rivers and other towns.

questions.q: Overpopulation occurs when:
options: The population exceeds the resources available to support it
A country has lots of empty land
Birth and death rates are equal
There are too few people to use resources fully
questions.explain: Overpopulation is when the number of people exceeds the resources and technology available to maintain a good standard of living.

questions.q: Which is an example of a 'pull' factor for migration?
options: Better job opportunities in the destination
questions.explain: Pull factors attract people to a new place; better jobs in the destination is a classic pull factor.

questions.q: Which physical factor tends to give a LOW population density?
options: High, rugged mountains with a harsh climate
questions.explain: Steep mountains, thin soils and harsh climates make farming and settlement difficult, leading to sparse populations.

questions.q: Underpopulation occurs when:
options: Birth and death rates are equal
A country has no natural resources
There are too few people to use the resources available effectively
questions.explain: Underpopulation is when a country has more resources than its population can fully use, often limiting economic development.

questions.q: A dispersed settlement pattern is one where:
options: Buildings are spread out and isolated
All houses are in one block
Buildings follow a road in a line
questions.explain: In a dispersed pattern, settlements are scattered and isolated, often in remote or upland farming areas.

questions.q: A youthful population (a high proportion of under-15s) often results from:
questions.explain: A high birth rate produces a large proportion of young people, giving a youthful population structure.

questions.q: Internal migration is defined as movement:
questions.explain: Internal migration is the movement of people within a country, such as rural-to-urban migration, rather than across borders.

questions.q: Which factor encourages a high population density?
options: Dense tropical rainforest with poor soils
A flat, fertile area with a temperate climate
questions.explain: Flat fertile land with a moderate climate supports farming and settlement, leading to higher population densities.

questions.q: On a settlement hierarchy, which has the highest order and largest range of services?
questions.explain: Cities and conurbations sit at the top of the settlement hierarchy with the largest populations and widest range of services.

questions.q: A benefit of immigration for a HOST country is often:
options: Filling labour shortages and adding skills
questions.explain: Immigrants can fill gaps in the labour market and bring skills, boosting the host country's economy.

questions.q: A pro-natalist population policy aims to:
options: Encourage couples to have more children
questions.explain: Pro-natalist policies use incentives such as benefits and childcare to raise birth rates in countries with ageing populations.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of a youthful population pyramid?
options: An equal width at every age
A narrow base and wide top
A wide base and narrow top
questions.explain: A youthful population has many children and few elderly, giving a pyramid with a wide base that narrows towards the top.

questions.q: In Stage 4 of the Demographic Transition Model, population is typically:
options: High and stable with low birth and death rates
questions.explain: In Stage 4 both birth and death rates are low, so the population is high and roughly stable.

questions.q: What is the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant?
options: A refugee is forced to flee, an economic migrant moves to seek work
An economic migrant is forced to flee persecution
A refugee always moves for a better job
questions.explain: Refugees are forced to leave to escape danger such as war or persecution, whereas economic migrants move to improve their living standards.

questions.q: The dependency ratio compares:
options: The non-working (young and old) population to the working-age population
questions.explain: The dependency ratio measures how many dependants (young and elderly) rely on each person of working age.

questions.q: Population density is best defined as:
options: The number of births each year
The total number of people in a country
The number of people per unit area
questions.explain: Population density measures how many people live in a given area, usually expressed as people per square kilometre.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Geography (2017) specification; Population Migration
